big_idea: Influence and persuasion are learnable, research-backed skills built on both broad frameworks and small, specific tactics, and this HBR collection's throughline is that emotional appeal, not just logic and data, is often what makes a persuasive message land.

tool.label: Cialdini's Principles of Persuasion (as applied in the collection)
tool.text: The anthology includes Robert Cialdini's Harnessing the Science of Persuasion, which lays out research-based levers of influence such as reciprocity, social proof, authority, consistency, liking, and scarcity. The collection frames these as tools to combine deliberately, for example pairing a small favor with visible evidence that respected peers already agree, rather than relying on any single lever alone.
tool.note: Cialdini's principles are broader work of his own reprinted and summarized in this HBR article; this booklet is not the original source of the framework, just one place it's collected.

ideas.title: Influence has identifiable components
ideas.text: One piece breaks influence down into specific components leaders can practice individually rather than treating it as one vague trait.

ideas.title: A handwritten note measurably increases compliance
ideas.text: One piece cites research that adding a small personal touch to a routine request significantly raises the odds someone follows through.

ideas.title: Charisma can be taught, not just inherited
ideas.text: Specific, learnable behaviors, like using rhetorical devices and confident nonverbal delivery, create the perception of charisma.

ideas.title: Storytelling changes how people receive information
ideas.text: A well-told story bypasses resistance that a fact-based pitch alone triggers, because it engages emotion alongside logic.

try_it: In your next request for help or buy-in, add one small personal touch, a handwritten note or a specific personal reference, rather than sending a generic ask.
Pick one recurring update or proposal and rewrite it once as pure data and once as a short story, then decide which fits the audience and stakes better.
best_for: Managers who want tactical, article-length techniques for a specific presentation, pitch, or negotiation
People who want Cialdini's persuasion research summarized alongside practical workplace applications
less_useful: Readers wanting a single coherent authorial voice or a from-scratch education in persuasion theory
Anyone uncomfortable with the collection's frank how-to-get-people-to-say-yes framing

related.why: Cialdini's full-length treatment of the same six persuasion principles
Cialdini's follow-up on shaping the moments right before an ask
